newsitem.title: TURKEY: Iraqi Kurd group says forming regional government.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi Kurd group says forming regional government.

text.p: The Iraqi Kurdish group that took control of northern Iraq in fighting with a rival group this month said on Thursday it was forming a 16-person cabinet to run affairs in the Kurdish region.

"The new administration includes representation of all peoples living in northern Iraq," said a statement by the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), which last month conquered the region with military help from Baghdad.
The statement said the cabinet, to be announced in the regional capital Arbil, will divide the posts among KDP, Assyrian Christian, Turcoman, Islamist and communist groups.

It said the Kurdish National Assembly -- composed of both KDP representatives and members of the defeated rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) -- met this month and appointed KDP politburo member Roj Nuri Shawyess as prime minister of the region.
But the PUK denounced the announcement.
"KDP's 'new cabinet' is reminiscent of Vichy's collaboration with the Nazis and it is no more than a desparate ploy that will fool no Kurd," the PUK said in a statement.
The PUK said the KDP had forced its members -- who were arrested during fighting last month -- to join the meeting in parliament.
"Under threats to their lives, many of the detained members were forced to participate in this sham," the statement said.
The PUK and KDP had shared power in an uneasy alliance after the 1991 Gulf War through 1994, when their local administration collapsed in fighting.
The PUK maintained that the original Kurdish parliament elected in 1992 -- equally divided between the two Kurdish groups -- was the only legitimate administration.

The entry of Iraqi forces into the north led to the collapse of a programme to assist Kurds in the region, which had been protected by a U.S.-led air force against attack from Baghdad since shortly after the Gulf War when Iraqi troops moved into the north to crush a Kurdish uprising.
